Magma is molten rock — that is, rock that has been heated to such extreme temperatures that it has melted into a hot, thick, flowing liquid — found beneath the Earth's surface, deep inside the planet.

Think of it this way: just as ice melts into water when heated, rock can melt too — it just needs far more heat to do so. The result of that melted rock is magma.
What Magma Actually Is

Magma is not simply pure liquid rock. It is a mixture of three things existing together at the same time:

  1. Molten (liquid) rock — the dominant part, mostly made of minerals containing silicon and oxygen, called silicates.
  2. Dissolved gases — magma contains gases trapped within it, mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide, in the same way that a fizzy drink holds dissolved carbon dioxide. These gases are invisible inside the magma but play a huge role in volcanic eruptions.
  3. Solid crystals — not all of the rock melts completely. Some minerals solidify into tiny crystals even while floating inside the hot liquid magma, especially as it slowly cools down.

So magma is like a thick, bubbling, partially crystallized liquid — not simply a clean molten liquid, but a complex mixture.
Where Magma Exists

Magma lives in the interior of the Earth, primarily in a layer called the mantle — the thick, rocky layer that sits beneath the Earth's outer shell (the crust) and extends deep into the planet.

It also collects in magma chambers — large underground reservoirs, or pockets, where magma pools and builds up over time. Picture a giant underground sponge soaked in molten rock rather than a hollow cave. These magma chambers sit beneath volcanoes and are the direct source of volcanic eruptions.
How Magma Forms

Rock melts and becomes magma under three conditions:

1. Extreme heat. The deeper you go into the Earth, the hotter it gets. The Earth's interior generates enormous heat from two main sources: leftover heat from when the planet formed billions of years ago, and heat produced by the natural decay of radioactive elements inside the Earth. At sufficient depths, this heat is intense enough to melt rock.

2. Drop in pressure. Rock has a melting point — the temperature at which it transitions from solid to liquid. That melting point is not fixed; it changes with pressure. When pressure decreases (for example, when two tectonic plates pull apart from each other), rock that was otherwise solid can suddenly melt, even without getting hotter.

3. Addition of water or other fluids. Water lowers the melting point of rock, the same way salt lowers the melting point of ice. When water seeps into hot rock deep underground — which happens, for instance, when one tectonic plate slides beneath another and carries water with it — the rock can melt at temperatures that would not ordinarily cause melting.

In nature, these three causes often work together.
Properties of Magma

Temperature: Magma is extraordinarily hot — typically between 700°C and 1,300°C (roughly 1,300°F to 2,400°F). For reference, your kitchen oven maxes out around 250°C. Magma is several times hotter than that.

Viscosity (thickness/flow): Magma can range from relatively runny to extremely thick and sticky, depending mainly on how much silica (a compound of silicon and oxygen) it contains and how hot it is.

  • High silica magma is very thick and sticky — it flows poorly, traps gases inside, and builds up enormous pressure, often leading to violent, explosive eruptions.
  • Low silica magma is thinner and runnier — it flows more freely, releases gases more easily, and tends to produce calmer eruptions that pour out lava in rivers.

This is why some volcanoes explode catastrophically while others simply ooze lava quietly. The difference largely comes down to the silica content of the magma beneath them.
How Magma Moves

Magma is less dense than the solid rock surrounding it, so it naturally tends to rise — the same reason a bubble of air rises through water. It slowly pushes upward through cracks, weak points, and fractures in the rock above it.

When conditions are right — enough pressure, a path to the surface — magma can rise all the way to the surface and erupt. This is a volcano.
Magma vs. Lava — A Critical Distinction

This is one of the most important things to understand about the word "magma":

Magma and lava are the same material. The word changes only based on location.

  • When the molten rock is underground, it is called magma.
  • The moment it reaches the Earth's surface and flows out of a volcano or crack in the ground, it is called lava.

Nothing chemically changes in that transition — it is purely a matter of where the molten rock is at any given moment. Once lava cools and solidifies on the surface, it becomes volcanic rock.
What Magma Becomes When It Cools

When magma cools and solidifies — whether underground or on the surface — it forms a category of rock called igneous rock (from the Latin word for fire, though you said to skip etymology — the key point is it means "fire-formed rock"). The nature of that rock depends on where and how fast the magma cooled:

  • Slow cooling underground (magma that never erupted) gives minerals a long time to grow into large crystals, forming coarse-grained rocks like granite. These are called intrusive igneous rocks because the magma intruded into existing rock and solidified there.
  • Fast cooling on the surface (lava that erupted) solidifies quickly, leaving no time for large crystals to grow. This produces fine-grained or even glassy rocks like basalt or obsidian. These are called extrusive igneous rocks.

Roughly speaking, the entire ocean floor is made of basalt — rock born from low-silica magma that poured out quietly along underwater volcanic ridges for billions of years.
Types of Magma

Magma is broadly classified by its silica content, which also predicts its behaviour:

Basaltic magma — lowest silica content (around 50%). This is the most common type on Earth. It is hot, runny, and flows easily. It produces relatively calm eruptions and forms the ocean floors and volcanic islands like Hawaii.

Andesitic magma — intermediate silica content (around 60%). More viscous than basaltic magma. Common at subduction zones — where one tectonic plate slides beneath another. It produces moderately explosive eruptions.

Rhyolitic magma — highest silica content (around 70%). Extremely thick and sticky. It traps gases powerfully and tends to erupt with tremendous, catastrophic explosions. Supervolcano eruptions — the rarest and most destructive kind — are associated with rhyolitic magma.
Why Magma Matters

Magma is not just an interesting geological curiosity — it is one of the fundamental forces that has shaped our planet:

  • It is the engine behind all volcanic activity on Earth.
  • It continuously creates new crust — particularly along mid-ocean ridges where plates pull apart and magma fills the gap, solidifying into fresh ocean floor.
  • It recycles the Earth's crust — old crust gets pulled down into the mantle, melts into magma, and can eventually erupt again, completing a planetary rock cycle that has run for billions of years.
  • It brings valuable minerals and metals — gold, silver, copper, and many other economically important materials are delivered to mineable depths through the movement of magma.
  • It influences climate — large volcanic eruptions inject gases and particles into the atmosphere that can cool the planet for years at a time.
  • Understanding how magma behaves is essential for predicting volcanic eruptions — which gases it releases, how viscous it is, and how fast it rises all help scientists forecast whether a volcano will erupt gently or explosively.
A Summary in One Paragraph

Magma is molten rock — a hot, thick, gas-rich liquid mixture — that exists beneath the Earth's surface, primarily in the mantle and in underground reservoirs called magma chambers. It forms when rock melts due to extreme heat, reduced pressure, or the presence of water. When it reaches the Earth's surface, it is called lava; when it cools and solidifies, it becomes igneous rock. Its silica content determines how runny or sticky it is, which in turn shapes the character of volcanic eruptions — from calm lava flows to catastrophic explosions. Magma is not merely a geological detail; it is one of the primary forces behind the creation, reshaping, and recycling of the Earth's crust over billions of years.
